:::{#exm-pois-deviance-residual}
#### Residuals for two observations

Suppose an observation has $y_i = 5$ events
and fitted mean $\ey_i = 2.5$.
Its Pearson residual is

$$
\ba
r_i
&\approx \frac{y_i - \ey_i}{\sqrt{\ey_i}}
&& \text{(Pearson residual)} \\
&= \frac{5 - 2.5}{\sqrt{2.5}}
&& \text{(substitute)} \\
&\approx 1.581
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\ea
$$

and by @thm-pois-deviance-residual its deviance residual is

$$
\ba
d_i
&= \signt(5 - 2.5) \sqrt{2\sb{5 \logf{\frac{5}{2.5}} - (5 - 2.5)}}
&& \text{(deviance residual formula)} \\
&= \sqrt{2\sb{5 \logf{2} - 2.5}}
&& \text{(} \signt(2.5) = 1 \text{; simplify)} \\
&\approx \sqrt{2\sb{3.466 - 2.5}}
&& \text{(} 5 \logf{2} \approx 3.466 \text{)} \\
&= \sqrt{1.931}
&& \text{(subtract and double)} \\
&\approx 1.390
&& \text{(square root)}
\ea
$$

An observation with $y_i = 0$ and the same fitted mean
has Pearson residual $-2.5 / \sqrt{2.5} \approx -1.581$
and deviance residual

$$
\ba
d_i
&= \signt(0 - 2.5) \sqrt{2\sb{0 - (0 - 2.5)}}
&& \text{(deviance residual formula with } y_i = 0 \text{)} \\
&= -\sqrt{5}
&& \text{(} \signt(-2.5) = -1 \text{; simplify)} \\
&\approx -2.236
&& \text{(square root)}
\ea
$$

The two Pearson residuals have equal magnitude,
but the deviance residuals do not.
The saturated model predicts an observed zero with probability 1,
so the fitted model loses more log-likelihood on the zero
than on the count of 5,
and the deviance residual of the zero is larger in magnitude.

:::
